680.title: The great collections, closed
680.hook: the Connected and the Numbered Sayings
680.howItsDone: Monastics in the Theravada tradition still memorize and chant suttas from the Connected and Numbered Sayings, and some lay study groups read them one short discourse at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three listeners and three pots, and your line, keep the pot upright. Did something stay in? Today we close a whole part of the path, and see what the pot holds. Day six hundred eighty.

Forty-five days ago this part of the path opened with two great libraries. The Samyutta Nikaya, the Connected Sayings. The Anguttara Nikaya, the Numbered Sayings. Together they hold thousands of short discourses, many no longer than a page. Long discourses are like novels. These are more like a box of letters: a question asked at a roadside, an image tossed off before a meal, a list counted on the fingers. Since then you've crossed the flood, seen Mara named, taken apart a chariot, felt the second arrow, watched foam on the river, and pulled your ears. Today we close both books. Today: samyutta.
screen: `TWO GREAT LIBRARIES.` → `A BOX OF SHORT LETTERS.` → `FORTY-FIVE DAYS.`

segments.voice: Start with how they're built, because that's the point of today's line. The Connected Sayings gathers its suttas by kind. Fifty-six groups, each on one theme or one speaker: a chapter of verses with gods, a chapter on Mara, a chapter on the five aggregates, one on the sense bases, one on mindfulness. Read it and you see a subject turned over a hundred ways. That's where you met the chariot of parts, the burden, the dog on its leash, all is burning, the eye as an ocean, the nuns and the inspiring sign, and the old Buddha in the sun. The Numbered Sayings gathers its suttas by number. The Book of Ones, the Book of Twos, all the way up to Elevens. Three intoxications. Four kinds of people, and the firebrand. Five remembrances. Five ways to remove a grudge. Six ways to be dear. Seven marks of a friend. Eight winds. Ten perceptions at a sick bed. Eleven blessings of metta. Why sort teaching by number? Tradition says these texts were passed on by memory, chanted by monks for generations before they were written down. A list of five is easier to carry than a paragraph. Each way of sorting shows you something. By kind, you go deep into one subject. By number, you get a toolkit, a handful of things to count on your fingers on an ordinary Tuesday. And across both, the same teacher keeps speaking to monks and nuns, kings and farmers, couples and the sick, in the plainest images he could find.
screen: `BY KIND: FIFTY-SIX GROUPS.` · `BY NUMBER: ONES TO ELEVENS.` · `MADE TO BE REMEMBERED.` · then, large: `BY KIND AND BY NUMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one line from each. Sit, and settle. Let the Connected Sayings pass by: the flood, the tangle, one arrow, foam on the river, the burden, all is burning, inspired then calm, even his. Which one stays? Hold it. Now let the Numbered Sayings pass: remember me as awake, for self and others, heir to my deeds, eight winds, toward less, sleep in peace, a friend gives the hard thing. Which one stays? Hold both lines together for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.

samyutta. The Pali word for connected or joined together, naming the Samyutta Nikaya: along with the Anguttara Nikaya, sorted by number, thousands of short discourses made to be remembered. Today's word.
Your line: by kind and by number. Today, carry your two chosen lines, one from each book, and say each once before bed. Tomorrow, a new part: the festival year. Day six hundred eighty.

screen: `DAY 680 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOON KEEPS THE CALENDAR.`

681.title: The moon keeps the calendar
681.hook: most Buddhist holy days fall on full and new moons; dates move each year
681.howItsDone: Across the Theravada world, lay Buddhists visit temples on full-moon and new-moon uposatha days, often keeping eight precepts, and monks recite the patimokkha on the full and new moons.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the great collections, and your line was by kind and by number. Which two lines did you keep? Today a new part of the path opens: the festival year. Day six hundred eighty-one.

Ask a Buddhist friend in Sri Lanka or Thailand when Vesak is this year, and they might have to check. Not because they've forgotten. Because it moves. Last year it was one date, next year another, sometimes weeks apart. Holidays pinned to a calendar square don't work that way. But for the early Buddhists, the calendar wasn't a grid on the wall. It was in the sky. Look up on a clear night and you can read it: full, half, new. For the next sixteen days, we walk through the Buddhist year. And it starts, fittingly, with the moon. Today: uposatha.
screen: `WHEN IS VESAK THIS YEAR?` → `IT MOVES.` → `THE CALENDAR IN THE SKY.`

segments.voice: In the Buddha's India, time was kept by the moon. A month ran from one full moon or new moon to the next. And the texts show the monks gathering on certain moon days, the full moon and the new moon, and in time the half moons too. These are uposatha days, observance days. On the full and new moon, monks gather to recite their rules together, the patimokkha. And lay people come to the monastery, listen to teaching, and some keep extra precepts for the day. That rhythm still beats across much of the Buddhist world. In Sri Lanka, every full moon day, called poya, is a public holiday. Then the big festivals sit on particular full moons. Vesak on one. The first sermon on another. The end of the rains retreat on another. Because a lunar year of twelve months is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, the festivals slide earlier each year, and every few years an extra month is added to pull them back. So the dates move, but the moon stays the same. Not every tradition keeps the moon. Japan moved to the solar calendar in the eighteen-seventies, and Japanese temples now generally mark the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on fixed solar dates. Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese communities generally keep the lunar dates. Different calendars, same stories. And one nice result of keeping the moon: anyone, anywhere, can look up and know roughly where they are in the holy year.
screen: `MONTHS FROM MOON TO MOON.` · `UPOSATHA: THE OBSERVANCE DAYS.` · `THE FESTIVALS SLIDE, THEN RESET.` · then, large: `THE MOON KEEPS THE CALENDAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find this year's full moons. Sit, and settle for a few breaths. Picture tonight's sky, and the moon wherever it is in its cycle. Is it waxing or waning? If you're not sure, that's fine. After the bell, look it up, or step outside tonight and see. Then find the next full moon and mark it. You might keep it as a quiet day: a little more stillness, a little more care. The bell holds the time.
uposatha. The Pali word for the observance day, kept on full and new moons, when most Buddhist holy days fall, so their dates move each year. Today's word.
Your line: look up, and know. Tonight, look for the moon, and say what phase it's in. Day six hundred eighty-one.

682.title: Vesak, deeper
682.hook: the triple blessed day; why Theravada lands keep birth, awakening and passing on one full moon
682.howItsDone: On Vesak, Buddhists in Theravada countries visit temples dressed in white, offer flowers, lights and incense, listen to teachings, keep the eight precepts for the day, and give food and drink freely at roadside stalls.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the uposatha days, and your line, look up, and know. Did you find the moon? Today, the May full moon, and Vesak. Day six hundred eighty-two.

You met Vesak in your first year on this path: one full moon that holds three events, the Buddha's birth, his awakening, and his passing away. Born, awake, gone. Today we go back, deeper, to Colombo on Vesak night. Streets strung with paper lanterns. Giant lit gateways, called thoranas, telling stories from the Buddha's past lives in painted scenes and colored bulbs. And along the roadsides, people handing out free food and drinks to anyone passing, strangers included. Those are dansal, stalls for giving. Nobody pays. Today: Vesak.
screen: `BORN, AWAKE, GONE.` → `LANTERNS AND THORANAS.` → `FREE FOOD FOR STRANGERS.`

segments.voice: Why one night for three events? In the Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, the commentaries place all three on the full moon of the month of Vesakha, which usually falls in May. Birth in the Lumbini garden. Awakening under the tree at Bodh Gaya, at thirty-five, tradition says. And the final passing at Kusinara, at eighty. That's the tradition's answer: they happened on the same moon. Not every tradition counts it that way. In much of East Asia, the three are kept on separate days: the birth in spring, the awakening in winter, the passing in early spring. In Tibet, they're honored together in Saga Dawa, a whole lunar month, which gets its own day later in this part. Different traditions, different reckonings. In the modern era, a step toward sharing the day: in 1950, Buddhists from many countries met in Sri Lanka and agreed to celebrate Vesak together on the full moon of May. And in 1999 the United Nations recognized the Day of Vesak. But under the lanterns, much of Vesak is quiet. People go to the temple dressed in white. They offer flowers, and a traditional verse of offering recalls that the flowers will fade. And some keep the eight precepts for the day: the usual five, plus not eating after noon, setting aside entertainment and adornment, and not using high, luxurious beds. A whole day lived a little like a monastic. Born, awake, gone: the festival holds a whole life, and invites one day of practice inside it.
screen: `THREE EVENTS, ONE FULL MOON.` · `OTHER TRADITIONS, OTHER DAYS.` · `1950: A SHARED DATE.` · then, large: `A DAY OF EIGHT PRECEPTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep eight precepts for a day. Not necessarily today; pick a day, perhaps the next full moon. Sit now, and settle. Walk through it in your mind. No harm to any living thing. Nothing taken that isn't given. No sexual activity. No false speech. No intoxicants. No food after noon. No entertainment or adornment. A simple bed. Notice which one you'd find hardest. Smile at that. Picture the day: quieter, simpler, roomier. The bell holds the time.
Vesak. The full moon of the month Vesakha, when Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on one night. Today's word.
Your line: born, awake, gone. Today, give one thing away freely, the way a dansal does, to someone who didn't ask. Day six hundred eighty-two.

683.title: Poson
683.hook: Sri Lanka's June full moon: Mahinda brings the teaching to the island
683.howItsDone: On Poson, Sri Lankan Buddhists make pilgrimage to Mihintale and Anuradhapura, dress in white, keep precepts, decorate streets with lanterns, and run dansal giving free food and drink.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vesak, the lanterns and the dansal, and your line, born, awake, gone. What did you give away? Today, one full moon later, a festival about how the teaching traveled. Day six hundred eighty-three.

A king is out hunting on a mountain. He's chasing a deer through the trees near his capital, the old city of Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka. The deer leads him up a slope, and then, the chronicle says, a voice calls him by his name. Tissa. Not his title. His name. Standing on a rock is a monk in robes, with companions, and the king has never seen anything like them. This is the story Sri Lankans tell on the June full moon, the day they call Poson, more than two thousand years later. The mountain is Mihintale. Today: Poson.
screen: `A KING HUNTING A DEER.` → `A VOICE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `A MONK ON A ROCK.`

segments.voice: The monk is Mahinda, and according to the Sri Lankan chronicles he's the son of Ashoka, the great Indian emperor who embraced the teaching. He has come, the chronicle says, to bring the Buddha's teaching to the island. But first, he tests the king. Not with a sermon. With a riddle. What is this tree called? A mango, says the king. Are there other mangoes besides this one? Many. And are there other trees besides this mango and the other mangoes? Many, but those aren't mangoes. And besides the other mangoes and the trees that aren't mangoes? This mango tree, sir. Then he asks the same thing about the king's relatives, and others who are not his relatives, and the king answers that too. Mahinda is satisfied. This man can think. Only then does he teach. The king, Devanampiya Tissa, comes to the teaching, and the chronicles describe the island turning toward it. Later, Mahinda's sister, the nun Sanghamitta, is said to have brought a cutting from the Bodhi tree, and a tree at Anuradhapura grown from it is still honored today. On Poson, pilgrims in white climb the long stairway at Mihintale, and families set up dansal along the roads, just like at Vesak. Notice what the festival honors. Not the Buddha's life this time. The moment the teaching arrived somewhere new, carried by a person, starting with a question about a mango tree.
screen: `MAHINDA, SON OF ASHOKA.` · `A RIDDLE ABOUT A MANGO TREE.` · `THEN THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `WHO BROUGHT IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall who brought the teaching to you. Sit, and settle. Ask yourself how any of this reached you: the teachings, this path, the habit of sitting still. Was it a person? A book, a teacher, a grandparent, a friend who mentioned it once? An app on a phone? Let a face come, or a moment. Picture them on the rock at Mihintale, calling your name. Let some thanks rise, whatever form it takes. The bell holds the time.
Poson. Sri Lanka's June full moon, when the arrival of the teaching with Mahinda at Mihintale is remembered. Today's word.
Your line: who brought it. Today, send a short thank-you to one person who first showed you something that changed you. Day six hundred eighty-three.

684.title: The rains begin
684.hook: Asalha Puja marks the first sermon; the rains retreat starts the next day
684.howItsDone: On Asalha Puja, Buddhists in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia gather at temples to hear the first sermon and circle the shrine with candles; during the following three-month Vassa, monks stay in one monastery and some lay people take on extra practices.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Poson, Mahinda and the mango tree, and your line, who brought it. Did you thank someone? Today, the next full moon, and two beginnings, one after the other. Day six hundred eighty-four.

In India, the monsoon doesn't drizzle. It arrives. Roads turn to rivers, fields to mud, and anything walking on the ground, worms, insects, frogs, comes up into the open. In the Buddha's time, wandering teachers of many kinds stopped traveling for these months. Buddhist monks, early on, kept walking. People complained, the Vinaya says: these monks trample the green shoots and crush small creatures. So the Buddha set a rule. Stay in one place for the rains. And the full moon just before the rains carries its own memory, the very first teaching. Today: vassa.

Start with the full moon. In the Theravada tradition, the full moon of the month Asalha, usually in July, is the anniversary of the first sermon. Two months after his awakening, tradition says, the Buddha found his five former companions in the Deer Park near Benares, and set the wheel of the teaching in motion: the middle way, the four noble truths. One of the five, Kondanna, understood, the first of them to see it. With that, the tradition says, the three jewels were complete: the Buddha, the teaching, and the community. Thailand, Laos and Cambodia mark the day as Asalha Puja, and in Thailand it's a national holiday. People go to the temple, hear the first sermon chanted, and walk three times around the shrine holding candles. Then, the very next day, the rains retreat begins: Vassa, a word that means rain, and also year, because a monk's seniority was counted in rains. For three lunar months, monks stay in one monastery. Some lay people take up something for the season too: giving up alcohol, keeping more precepts, meditating daily, coming to the temple on every moon day. In Thailand, it's a custom for young men to ordain for one Vassa, as a rite of passage. And for a monastery, it's the quiet season, the time for study and practice, with nowhere to go. There's a gentle wisdom in it. Weather you can't change becomes a season you use.
screen: `THE FIRST SERMON'S FULL MOON.` · `KONDANNA UNDERSTANDS.` · `VASSA: THREE MONTHS IN ONE PLACE.` · then, large: `THE RAINS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin a three-month practice. Sit, and settle. Ask yourself: what could I keep for one season? Something small enough to last. Five minutes of sitting each morning. No phone in bed. One kind message a week. Fewer drinks. Let a few options come, and notice which one feels right, not heroic. Picture yourself three months from now, having kept it. Choose it, quietly, here. The bell holds the time.
vassa. The Pali word for rain, the rainy season, and a year: Asalha Puja remembers the first sermon on the full moon, and the next day the three-month rains retreat begins. Today's word.
Your line: choose this season's practice. Today, write down your three-month practice and the date it ends. Day six hundred eighty-four.

685.title: The tooth relic procession
685.hook: Kandy's Esala Perahera: drummers, dancers, elephants, the relic casket
685.howItsDone: Each year around the Esala full moon, crowds gather in Kandy to watch the Perahera, and Buddhists visit the Temple of the Tooth to offer flowers and pay respects at the shrine of the relic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first sermon and the rains retreat, and your line, choose this season's practice. Did you choose a practice for the season? Today, back to Sri Lanka, for a night of drums and elephants. Day six hundred eighty-five.

First you hear the whips. Men walk ahead cracking long whips against the road, a sound like gunshots, to clear the way. Then fire-ball twirlers. Then drums, dozens of them, and Kandyan dancers in silver headdresses, spinning. Then elephants, draped in cloth covered with lights, walking slowly through the streets of Kandy, in the hills of Sri Lanka. And then the one everyone waits for: a great tusker, carrying on its back a golden casket under a canopy. The crowd goes quiet, hands pressed together. Today: datha.
screen: `WHIPS CRACK TO CLEAR THE WAY.` → `DRUMS, DANCERS, ELEPHANTS.` → `THE TUSKER WITH THE CASKET.`

segments.voice: Inside the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy is a relic Sri Lankans honor as a tooth of the Buddha. The tradition says that after his cremation at Kusinara, a tooth was saved, and centuries later, around the fourth century, it was carried to Sri Lanka from the kingdom of Kalinga by a princess named Hemamala, hidden in her hair, with her husband, Prince Danta. In time, the chronicles link holding the tooth with the right to rule, and the relic moved with the royal capital until it came to rest in Kandy. Every year, around the Esala full moon in July or August, the Esala Perahera fills the city for about ten nights. The procession has older roots too: it also honors guardian deities whose shrines stand near the temple, and their own processions walk behind. Each night, the main tusker carries the casket. The festival honors what the relic stands for: the Buddha's presence among people, and, in local tradition, protection and timely rain for the crops. Scholars, and some Buddhists, add a quiet caution: no one can prove the tooth's history. But the procession isn't a museum label. Tradition treats it as the Buddha's presence passing through the streets, and people on the curb raise their hands as it goes by. A relic doesn't sit still in a glass case here. Once a year, it walks.
screen: `A TOOTH OF THE BUDDHA.` · `HIDDEN IN A PRINCESS'S HAIR.` · `TEN NIGHTS IN KANDY.` · then, large: `THE RELIC WALKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the procession. Sit, and close your eyes. Hear the drums start, far off, and come closer. See the dancers, the torches, the lights on the elephants. Feel the crowd around you, the warm night air. Now the tusker comes, slow and huge, the casket glowing on its back. Let the noise drop away. Put your palms together, if you like, and join the crowd's stillness for a moment. Then let the procession pass, and sit in the quiet it leaves. The bell holds the time.
datha. The Pali word for a tooth, behind Kandy's Esala Perahera: drummers, dancers and elephants carrying the casket of the Buddha's tooth relic through the streets. Today's word.
Your line: the relic walks. Today, carry something that reminds you of a person you honor, and let it walk with you. Day six hundred eighty-five.

686.title: Obon
686.hook: in Japan a summer festival welcoming ancestors home, linked to the story of Moggallana helping his mother (Ullambana)
686.howItsDone: During Obon, Japanese families return to their hometowns, clean and visit graves, make offerings at home altars, invite priests to chant, dance the Bon Odori, and light fires or float lanterns to welcome and send off ancestors.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Perahera in Kandy, and your line, the relic walks. What walked with you? Today closes a week, and travels to Japan in midsummer. Day six hundred eighty-six.

This week we closed the great collections and stepped into the festival year: the moon calendar, Vesak's lanterns, Mahinda on the mountain, the rains, the tooth on the tusker's back. Now it's August in Japan. Trains are packed with people going home, to the towns where their families come from. At dusk, outside the houses, small fires are lit by the door. They're welcome fires, called mukaebi, so the spirits of the family's dead can find their way back. For a few days, the ancestors are guests. Today: Obon.
screen: `A WEEK OF FESTIVALS.` → `PACKED TRAINS HOME.` → `FIRES BY THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Obon, often just called Bon, traces back to a story told in a Chinese Buddhist scripture, the Ullambana Sutra. In it, Moggallana, the disciple famous for his powers of mind, the same one you saw nodding off and pulling his ears, uses those powers to look for his dead mother. He finds her reborn among the hungry ghosts, starving. He brings her a bowl of rice, but as it touches her mouth, it bursts into flame. Heartbroken, he goes to the Buddha. The Buddha tells him that on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the rains retreat ends, he should make offerings to the whole community of monks; the merit of that gift can reach seven generations of ancestors. Moggallana does it, and his mother is freed. Scholars note that this scripture appears to have been composed in China, not translated from an Indian original; it doesn't appear in the Pali canon. But it shaped festivals across East Asia. In Japan, families clean graves, set out food and flowers at home altars, and invite a priest to chant. In the evenings, whole neighborhoods dance the Bon Odori in circles, some say born from Moggallana's joy. And at the end, the spirits are sent off: with farewell fires, like the giant characters lit on the mountains around Kyoto, or with paper lanterns floated down rivers to the sea. Welcome them, feed them, dance, send them home. The dead, for a few days, are family at the table.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a lamp for an ancestor. If you have a candle or a small light, light it now. If not, picture one. Sit, and let its glow settle you. Bring to mind someone in your family who has died, a grandparent, a parent, someone further back whose name you only heard. If none comes, think of all the people who came before you.
